meta.title: Irish Phrases and Expressions
meta.subtitle: 613 expressions · 117 everyday, 294 expressions, 149 verb phrases, 23 idioms, 30 proverbs · both directions
meta.desc: 613 Irish set phrases, expressions, verb phrases, idioms and proverbs, in five subdecks: 117 everyday phrases, 294 expressions, 149 verb phrases, 23 idioms and 30 proverbs. Both study directions come as two cards of one expression — Irish → English (see the Irish, recall the meaning) and English → Irish (see an English meaning, recall the Irish) — each with a schedule of its own. This is a companion to the five level decks, Irish A1 to C1, and not one of them: a level is a list of words, and an expression is a unit a list of words cannot see. Nothing here is taught by any of the five, so the two can be studied together without repeating an entry. The PHRASES are the expressions Wiktionary files as phrases or interjections — mostly the everyday formulas an Irish speaker uses as one piece (is féidir, is fearr, sin é …). The EXPRESSIONS are the adverbial, prepositional and joining expressions Irish builds out of a preposition and a noun (ar bith, a chlog, aon duine …), which a learner meets on every page. The VERB PHRASES are a verb with a preposition or an adverb that together mean something the verb alone does not (ba mhaith le, bain as, bí ar …). The IDIOMS are the expressions Wiktionary marks as idiomatic (ar buile, ar bís, ó mo chroí amach …) — few, because few Irish idioms are marked — and the PROVERBS the sayings it files as proverbs (bíonn cluasa ar an gcoill, aithníonn ciaróg ciaróg eile, folaíonn grá gráin …). Within each subdeck the expressions come in the order of how many of Tatoeba's Irish sentences contain them, every word in any of its mutated spellings; 106 of the 613 are found there, and the rest follow in the order of how common their words are in the Irish Wikipedia. Real example sentences come with 97 of the 613 expressions, three apiece for 26, with the expression picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword; few devices have an Irish voice, so the speaker may be silent. Sources. Expressions, meanings and the idiom and proverb labels: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Order: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR, then the Irish Wikipedia (ga.wikipedia.org), its articles as of 1 November 2026, counted for this deck (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba, CC BY 2.0 FR.
